title: Ultrasound in Primary Care: Use the Modality for the Question It Answers Best
bottomLine: Ultrasound is valuable when it can answer a focused question without ionizing radiation—biliary, pelvic/pregnancy, effusion, bladder, DVT and selected soft-tissue questions—but a limited or negative study must not overrule a dangerous clinical syndrome when sensitivity is insufficient.
recognize: Ultrasound is operator- and body-habitus dependent and answers some questions far better than others.
Point-of-care ultrasound supplements the clinical assessment; it does not replace formal imaging or specialist interpretation when the question exceeds the operator's validated scope.
differentiate: A negative bedside scan does not safely exclude every PE, appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy or vascular emergency.
Formal diagnostic ultrasound and focused POCUS have different documentation, quality and credentialing expectations.
assessment: Define the clinical question, urgency, pregnancy/radiation considerations and whether a positive/negative result will actually change management.
workup: Escalate to formal ultrasound, CT/MRI or specialty evaluation when the bedside study is indeterminate or the clinical risk remains high.
management: Use findings within validated scope and local policy; stabilize emergencies rather than delaying for an optional scan.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary sedation/contrast by choosing ultrasound when it can answer the question, but do not avoid necessary definitive imaging solely to eliminate radiation.
redFlags: Persistent high-risk DVT/ectopic concern despite nondiagnostic scan
Operator uncertainty in an unstable patient
counselling: Explain what the ultrasound can and cannot determine and why another test may still be needed.
followUp: Document limitations and ensure formal follow-up for indeterminate or incidental findings.
examTrap: Using a limited POCUS result as definitive exclusion of a high-risk diagnosis outside the test's validated performance.
oneLinePearl: Ultrasound is strongest when the question is focused and the operator knows the limits.

title: CT: Use Speed and Detail When the Benefit Justifies Radiation and Contrast
bottomLine: CT is fast and highly useful for many emergency thoracic, abdominal, neurologic and traumatic questions, but it should be selected for a specific diagnosis that changes care. Radiation, pregnancy, renal/contrast issues and prior imaging matter, yet outdated blanket 'contraindications' should not delay life-saving imaging.
recognize: Noncontrast, contrast-enhanced, angiographic and low-dose CT protocols answer different questions.
Children and pregnancy require extra attention to radiation alternatives, but urgency and diagnostic benefit still govern.
differentiate: CT is not automatically superior to ultrasound or MRI; modality choice depends on anatomy, urgency and the suspected disease.
Contrast risk is individualized; prior mild reaction or CKD does not automatically prohibit all contrast-enhanced CT.
assessment: Define indication, pregnancy possibility, renal function when contrast decisions require it, prior contrast reaction and whether previous imaging already answers the question.
workup: Choose the correct protocol and avoid repeat CT when recent adequate imaging exists unless the clinical question changed.
management: Proceed urgently when benefit outweighs risk; use alternative imaging when it provides equivalent information with less harm.
medicationSafety: Contrast premedication and medication holds are protocol/patient specific; use current radiology guidance rather than universal rules.
redFlags: High-risk PE when CT angiography is appropriate
counselling: Explain why CT is being used, including radiation/contrast tradeoffs when time allows.
followUp: Track incidental findings and radiology recommendations to completion.
examTrap: Avoiding an urgently indicated CT because of a generalized fear of contrast/radiation without weighing immediate diagnostic benefit.
oneLinePearl: CT is a question-specific tool; protocol and urgency matter as much as the scanner.

title: MRI: High Soft-Tissue Detail, Strong Safety Screening, and the Right Urgency
bottomLine: MRI offers excellent neurologic, spinal, soft-tissue and many organ-specific assessments without ionizing radiation, but it is slower, less available and requires device/metal/claustrophobia safety screening. Do not delay a time-critical CT-based emergency pathway simply because MRI is more sensitive for another question.
recognize: MRI is particularly useful for brain/spinal cord, demyelination, soft tissue, marrow and selected abdominal/pelvic questions.
Implanted devices are not automatically unsafe; MRI-conditional status and protocol determine eligibility.
differentiate: MRI is not the initial test for every acute head/trauma/bleeding presentation.
Gadolinium contrast and MRI device safety are different issues and require separate assessment.
assessment: Screen implanted devices/metal, prior surgery/foreign bodies, claustrophobia, ability to lie still, pregnancy and renal function when gadolinium is planned.
workup: Choose MRI sequence/contrast according to the clinical question and use urgent alternative imaging when MRI delay would harm.
management: Coordinate device verification/sedation when needed and act urgently on cord compression, abscess, cauda equina or other critical findings.
medicationSafety: Sedation risk and gadolinium decisions are individualized; avoid routine sedation when communication/support can achieve the scan safely.
redFlags: Device status unknown with urgent MRI request
Unstable patient who cannot safely tolerate scanner delay
counselling: Explain the magnetic-field/device questions and why another modality may be safer/faster in some emergencies.
followUp: Track critical/incidental findings and required specialist referral.
examTrap: Waiting for MRI in a time-sensitive condition when a faster validated emergency imaging pathway should happen first.
oneLinePearl: MRI is powerful because of tissue contrast, not because it is always the best first test.
sourceBasis: Canadian radiology safety and imaging practice

title: Nuclear Medicine: Functional Imaging Needs a Specific Physiologic Question
bottomLine: Nuclear medicine studies assess physiology, perfusion, metabolism or receptor uptake and should be ordered only when that functional information changes care. The tracer, pregnancy/lactation status, timing and alternative imaging matter; a nuclear study is not a generic replacement for CT/MRI/ultrasound.
recognize: Examples include V/Q scanning, myocardial perfusion, thyroid uptake, bone scans and PET-based oncologic imaging.
Different tracers and protocols answer different questions and have different preparation requirements.
differentiate: V/Q imaging can be useful when CT pulmonary angiography is unsuitable or local algorithms prefer it in selected patients.
PET uptake is not cancer-specific; infection/inflammation can also be metabolically active.
assessment: Clarify indication, pregnancy/lactation, renal function where relevant, prior imaging and medication/preparation requirements.
workup: Use specialty/radiology protocol to select the tracer and interpret the result alongside anatomic imaging and pretest probability.
management: Act on the diagnosis the study supports rather than treating uptake itself.
medicationSafety: Medication/iodine/thyroid preparation can alter some studies; verify protocol-specific requirements.
redFlags: Unstable patient needing faster definitive imaging
High-risk result requiring immediate specialty action
counselling: Explain the purpose of tracer-based functional imaging and any temporary radiation precautions.
followUp: Ensure result integration with the definitive diagnostic/treatment pathway.
examTrap: Ordering a nuclear study because it is 'more advanced' without identifying the physiologic question it answers.
oneLinePearl: Nuclear medicine maps function; order it when function changes the decision.

title: Screening Tests: Apply Them to the Right Asymptomatic Population
bottomLine: Screening is for asymptomatic people at defined risk. Interpret a screening result through prevalence, test characteristics and the downstream diagnostic pathway; symptoms or prior abnormalities move the patient out of routine screening into diagnostic evaluation.
recognize: Positive predictive value changes with disease prevalence and patient risk even when sensitivity/specificity are unchanged.
A positive screen is not a final diagnosis and a negative screen does not overrule concerning symptoms.
differentiate: Screening, surveillance and diagnosis are different clinical tasks.
Program eligibility/funding can differ from national evidence recommendations.
assessment: Confirm asymptomatic status, anatomy, age/risk, prior results, life expectancy/ability to benefit, family/genetic risk and access to follow-up.
workup: Use the current national/provincial screening pathway and its confirmatory testing sequence.
management: Offer evidence-based screening with shared decision-making where benefits/harms are preference sensitive and ensure abnormal results reach diagnostic resolution.
medicationSafety: Avoid pre-emptive treatment before the abnormal screen is confirmed unless a validated pathway specifically requires it.
redFlags: Symptoms being incorrectly routed to screening
High-risk family/genetic syndrome needing a different pathway
counselling: Explain false positives, false negatives and overdiagnosis in terms relevant to the actual test.
followUp: Track abnormal screening until definitive diagnostic closure.
examTrap: Using a routine screening test as the evaluation for a symptomatic patient.
sourceBasis: Canadian preventive health and provincial screening program principles

title: Sensitivity and Specificity: Pretest Probability Determines What a Result Means
bottomLine: Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance under defined conditions; they do not directly tell you the probability that this individual patient has disease. Combine pretest probability with likelihood ratios/results to estimate post-test probability and decide whether to rule out, confirm or test further.
recognize: High sensitivity can be useful for ruling out when the test is negative in an appropriate low/intermediate-risk setting; high specificity can support ruling in when positive.
Predictive values change with prevalence/pretest probability.
differentiate: A highly sensitive test is not automatically a good screening test if harms, false positives or feasibility are unacceptable.
A negative test cannot safely rule out disease when pretest probability is very high and the test is imperfect.
assessment: Estimate pretest probability before ordering the test and identify the treatment/testing threshold that matters clinically.
workup: Use validated clinical decision rules only in the populations/settings for which they were developed.
management: Choose testing only when the result can move probability across a meaningful decision threshold.
medicationSafety: Avoid exposing patients to treatment toxicity solely because a low-specificity test is positive without confirmatory evidence.
redFlags: High-risk disease being falsely dismissed after an insufficiently sensitive test
Low-risk patient harmed by cascades after indiscriminate testing
counselling: Explain uncertainty and why another test may or may not be useful after an initial result.
followUp: Reassess probability when new clinical information changes the pretest picture.
examTrap: Interpreting a positive result as the same disease probability in a low-risk screening population and a high-risk symptomatic population.
oneLinePearl: Test performance is fixed; what the result means changes with pretest probability.

title: Point-of-Care Testing: Fast Results Still Need Quality Control and Confirmation
bottomLine: Point-of-care testing is valuable when speed changes care, but analytic limits, specimen quality, operator competence and confirmatory requirements still apply. A surprising or high-consequence result should be reconciled with the clinical picture and laboratory confirmation when the device/pathway requires it.
recognize: POC glucose, pregnancy, urinalysis, respiratory pathogen, INR and selected chemistry tests can accelerate decisions.
Device performance and quality-control requirements vary substantially.
differentiate: A rapid screening result may be preliminary and may not have the same sensitivity/specificity as central laboratory testing.
Near-patient testing is not exempt from documentation, QC or infection-control requirements.
assessment: Confirm the test is validated for the patient/specimen/context and that the result will alter immediate management.
workup: Repeat or confirm discordant, implausible or high-consequence results according to the device and local laboratory policy.
management: Act immediately on validated emergency results while arranging confirmatory testing when necessary.
medicationSafety: Do not make irreversible medication decisions from an implausible POC result without checking device/specimen limitations.
redFlags: Critical result inconsistent with the patient
counselling: Explain when a rapid result is final versus preliminary and why confirmation may be required.
followUp: Document result, QC/confirmation pathway and responsibility for pending central-lab results.
examTrap: Assuming a fast result is automatically a more reliable result.
oneLinePearl: POC testing buys time—not immunity from quality standards.
sourceBasis: Canadian laboratory medicine and point-of-care quality principles

title: Microbiology Results: Infection, Colonization, Contamination, or Prior Exposure?
bottomLine: Microbiology results must be interpreted with specimen site/quality, symptoms, host risk and pretest probability. A positive test can represent infection, colonization, contamination or residual nucleic acid/antibody, while a negative test may reflect timing or sampling limitations.
recognize: Sterile-site growth generally has different significance from colonized-site cultures.
NAAT, culture, antigen and serology detect different biological signals and have different windows of positivity.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not symptomatic UTI in most nonpregnant adults.
A positive respiratory/wound culture can represent colonization when the clinical syndrome does not support infection.
assessment: Define symptoms/source, immune status, prior antimicrobials, specimen quality/timing and whether the organism fits the syndrome.
workup: Repeat or obtain better specimens when contamination/poor quality is likely; use susceptibility testing and source-specific diagnostics when they change treatment.
management: Treat the patient/syndrome and source control, not the laboratory name alone; narrow/stop antimicrobials when evidence shows colonization or an alternate diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antimicrobial treatment causes resistance and adverse effects; drug selection should incorporate susceptibility, site penetration and organ function.
redFlags: Positive blood/CSF/other sterile-site result with compatible illness
counselling: Explain why a positive culture does not always require antibiotics and why some tests remain positive after infection resolves.
followUp: Review pending cultures/susceptibilities and public-health actions to completion.
examTrap: Treating a positive culture without first deciding whether the organism is causing the patient's syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Microbiology answers what was detected; clinical reasoning decides whether it is disease.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical Microbiology recommendations
